newsitem.title: JAPAN: Fears for Japan's coastline grow from oil spill.
newsitem.headline: Fears for Japan's coastline grow from oil spill.

text.p: Japanese officials said on Saturday they were increasingly worried that oil from a ruptured Russian tanker could hit fertile fishing areas along Japan's northern coast.
An estimated 4,700 tonnes (33,000 barrels) of fuel oil have escaped from the vessel, authorities said. But with heavy seas they lost track of an earlier oil slick.
"We sent out two helicopters today but they haven't managed to locate any oil slicks because of the stormy weather," a spokesman for Japan's Maritime Safety Agency said.
He added that nine ships would be dispatched to the area in an attempt to break up the oil before it gets to the coast.
"There may be great damage to the local coastal environment, especially to the shellfish population, if the slick hits," he said.
The 1.8 km (1.1 miles) long oil slick was last seen on Friday, 137 km (82 miles) from the Japanese coast.

The Russian-registered Nakhodka, built 26 years ago, broke up in heavy seas on Thursday. Authorities said the age of the ship, which was heading for Russia from China, was probably responsible for the accident.
The 31 crew members from the tanker were rescued on Thursday despite the rough seas but the captain was still missing. Officials said there was almost no hope that he survived.
With southeasterly winds, the Maritime agency fears the spilt oil may reach the coastline in the next few days.
Officials are also worried about the oil still aboard in unruptured tanks. The vessel was carrying 19,000 tonnes (133,000 barrels) of grade C heavy oil.

But they said that with the heavy weather, which helps to break up the oil, and the relatively long distance from the coast it was too soon to say if the accident would create a serious environmental disaster.

Any spill hitting the coast would be a major blow to the region. Shellfish are a speciality of the 300 kilometre (180-mile) swathe of picturesque coastline, which is dotted with fishing villages along the central part of Japan's main island of Honshu.
Fishing remains a major industry in Japan. Seafood is a mainstay of the Japanese diet and closely tied to its history and culture.
Despite its heavy reliance on imported oil, Japan has avoided any of the large-scale environmental disasters that have hit elsewhere.
Its worst oil accident occurred in 1974 when 7,900 tonnes (55,000 barrels) of oil leaked from an oil platform operated by Mitsubishi Oil Co.
By comparison, the 1989 Exxon Valdez disaster poured an estimated 37,000 tonnes (260,000 barrels) into Alaskan waters.
